title: How does Flink compare to Spark Structured Streaming (true record-at-a-time vs micro-batch, native event-time support, lower latency, richer state primitives in Flink vs Spark's larger ecosystem and batch-first design)?
shortTitle: How does Flink compare to Spark Structured Streaming

s1_definition.profdef: Apache Flink and Spark Structured Streaming are both distributed stream-processing engines, but they come from opposite design philosophies. Flink is streaming-first, processing events one record at a time with native event-time semantics, very low latency, and rich stateful primitives like keyed state and timers. Spark Structured Streaming is batch-first, processing streams as a series of small micro-batches on the Spark engine, which gives slightly higher latency but a unified batch-and-stream API and a very large ecosystem. You choose Flink for the lowest-latency, most sophisticated stateful streaming, and Spark when you want one engine and ecosystem spanning heavy batch, machine learning, and streaming together.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India processing incoming transactions. Flink is like a dedicated real-time officer who handles each transaction the instant it arrives, keeping detailed personal notes and reminders for every customer, so alerts fire in milliseconds. Spark Structured Streaming is like a clerk who collects transactions into small stacks every second and processes each stack together; it is a touch slower because it waits to form each stack, but this clerk also happens to be the same person who runs the bank's big nightly batch reports and its analytics, so using one versatile clerk for everything is operationally simpler. Flink optimizes for instant, stateful reaction; Spark optimizes for one unified engine across batch and stream.
s1_definition.oneliner: Flink is streaming-first with true record-at-a-time processing, native event time, lower latency, and richer state, while Spark Structured Streaming is batch-first with micro-batches, a unified batch-and-stream API, and a larger ecosystem.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Apache Flink and Spark Structured Streaming are both distributed stream-processing engines, but they come from opposite design philosophies. Flink is streaming-first, processing events one record at a time with native event-time semantics, very low latency, and rich stateful primitives like keyed state and timers. Spark Structured Streaming is batch-first, processing streams as a series of small micro-batches on the Spark engine, which gives slightly higher latency but a unified batch-and-stream API and a very large ecosystem. You choose Flink for the lowest-latency, most sophisticated stateful streaming, and Spark when you want one engine and ecosystem spanning heavy batch, machine learning, and streaming together.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India processing incoming transactions. Flink is like a dedicated real-time officer who handles each transaction the instant it arrives, keeping detailed personal notes and reminders for every customer, so alerts fire in milliseconds. Spark Structured Streaming is like a clerk who collects transactions into small stacks every second and processes each stack together; it is a touch slower because it waits to form each stack, but this clerk also happens to be the same person who runs the bank's big nightly batch reports and its analytics, so using one versatile clerk for everything is operationally simpler. Flink optimizes for instant, stateful reaction; Spark optimizes for one unified engine across batch and stream.

**One line to remember:** Flink is streaming-first with true record-at-a-time processing, native event time, lower latency, and richer state, while Spark Structured Streaming is batch-first with micro-batches, a unified batch-and-stream API, and a larger ecosystem.

sections.s2_technical:
The deepest difference is the processing model. Flink is a true streaming engine: each event flows through the operators as soon as it arrives and is processed individually, so end-to-end latency can be in the single-digit or tens of milliseconds. Spark Structured Streaming, by default, uses micro-batching: it collects records arriving over a short interval into a small batch and runs that batch through the Spark engine, so latency is bounded by the batch interval, typically hundreds of milliseconds to a few seconds. Spark later added a continuous processing mode that approaches record-at-a-time, but it is experimental and limited, so in practice Spark streaming is micro-batch. For most analytics and even many fraud use cases, micro-batch latency is perfectly acceptable; for ultra-low-latency needs, Flink's true streaming wins.

Event-time handling and state are the next big differences. Flink was built around event time from the start, with first-class watermarks, event-time timers, and sophisticated windowing including session windows, and it exposes rich keyed-state primitives, value state, list state, map state, and precise timer control through process functions, so complex stateful logic like custom state machines and fine-grained temporal rules is natural. Spark Structured Streaming also supports event time and watermarks and stateful operations like windowed aggregations, stream-stream joins, and arbitrary stateful processing through its state APIs, and these are good, but the state model and timer control are less granular than Flink's, and some complex patterns are harder to express. Flink also has mature, flexible checkpointing with incremental checkpoints and savepoints for upgrades, giving strong exactly-once guarantees with low overhead, while Spark achieves exactly-once through checkpointed offsets and idempotent sinks within the micro-batch model.

The counterweight is Spark's ecosystem and unification. Spark is batch-first and the streaming API is the same DataFrame and SQL API as batch, so a team already using Spark for heavy batch ETL, Spark SQL analytics, and MLlib or Spark ML gets streaming as an extension of the same engine, the same code, and the same skills, which is a major operational advantage. Spark has a larger community, more connectors, deep integration with Databricks and Delta Lake, and is often already in place, so adopting Structured Streaming adds no new engine. Flink, being streaming-first, is the specialist you bring in when streaming is central and demanding, though Flink also does batch well and is unifying the two. A senior-level nuance is that the choice is rarely about raw capability, since both can do most streaming tasks, but about fit: pick Flink when you need the lowest latency, the richest state and event-time semantics, or complex event processing, and pick Spark Structured Streaming when you want one engine and one skill set across batch, analytics, machine learning, and streaming, or you are already invested in the Spark and Databricks ecosystem. Another nuance is operational maturity in your organization: running Flink well is its own skill, while a Spark shop can extend into streaming with less new operational burden. The practical rule at a bank is to use Flink for the hard real-time, heavily stateful streaming like sub-second fraud reaction, and Spark Structured Streaming for streaming that lives alongside the bank's large batch and analytics workloads where unification and the existing ecosystem matter more than the last few milliseconds of latency.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, two streaming needs arose. One is sub-second fraud reaction on the live transaction stream, where every millisecond of delay matters and the logic needs detailed per-account state and timers. The other is a near-real-time dashboard of transaction volumes that sits alongside the bank's existing heavy Spark batch and analytics stack. Choosing one engine for both would compromise one of them. This is exactly the comparison: Flink's true record-at-a-time, rich-state model fits the fraud reaction, while Spark Structured Streaming's micro-batch model and ecosystem unification fit the dashboard.

This is exactly how Flink and Spark Structured Streaming compare. Flink processes each event immediately with low latency and rich state, suiting the fraud case, and Spark processes micro-batches on the same engine as its batch and analytics, suiting the dashboard.

Problem 2 — The team wanted to quantify the latency difference and understand the state-model difference to justify using two engines. Flink emits an alert on the event itself, while Spark waits to fill a micro-batch before emitting, and Flink's per-key timer state expresses a rule that is clumsier in Spark. This is the latency and state-primitive contrast.

Because running real Flink and Spark clusters is heavy, this runnable demo models both engines' processing behavior. A `FlinkEngine` processes each event immediately, keeping rich per-key state and emitting with minimal simulated latency. A `SparkStructuredStreaming` buffers events into micro-batches of a fixed interval and emits per batch with the batch interval as latency. A `LatencyComparer` runs the same transaction stream through both and reports per-event latency and the state-model difference. The demo shows Flink's lower, per-event latency and richer state versus Spark's micro-batch latency and unified-engine simplicity.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five transactions arriving over about one and a third seconds, two for Rajesh's account, two for Priya's account including a very large one, and one more for Rajesh.

Step 1: In the Flink engine each event is processed the instant it arrives. For every transaction the engine emits a result about five milliseconds after arrival and immediately updates rich per-account state holding a running count and sum, so after Rajesh's third transaction the state shows his count and total up to date.

Step 2: Because Flink emits per event with only a few milliseconds of processing delay, every transaction's latency is tiny, so the average latency is a handful of milliseconds, suiting sub-second fraud reaction.

Step 3: In the Spark Structured Streaming engine the events are buffered into micro-batches of one second. The first batch collects the transactions arriving in the first second and emits them together at the one-second boundary, and the remaining transactions form the next batch emitted at the two-second boundary.

Step 4: Because each event waits for its micro-batch to close before being emitted, an event that arrived early in a batch waits almost the full interval, so the average latency is on the order of hundreds of milliseconds, bounded by the batch interval. The log notes that this runs on the same DataFrame and SQL engine Spark uses for batch, which is the unification benefit.

Step 5: The comparer reports both average latencies side by side, Flink's few milliseconds against Spark's hundreds, and summarizes the state-model difference: Flink offers rich keyed state and per-event timers, while Spark offers windowed and arbitrary stateful processing on micro-batches unified with its batch, SQL, and machine-learning stack.

Step 6: The guidance line concludes that Flink fits sub-second, heavily stateful fraud reaction, while Spark Structured Streaming fits streaming that lives alongside the bank's batch and analytics in one ecosystem.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Flink and Spark Structured Streaming are both distributed stream processors, but they start from opposite philosophies, and that drives the whole comparison. Flink is streaming-first: it processes events one record at a time, so each event flows through the operators the instant it arrives and end-to-end latency can be in the single-digit or tens of milliseconds. Spark Structured Streaming is batch-first: by default it collects records over a short interval into a micro-batch and runs that batch through the Spark engine, so latency is bounded by the batch interval, typically hundreds of milliseconds to a few seconds. Spark added an experimental continuous mode that approaches record-at-a-time, but in practice Spark streaming is micro-batch. Flink was also built around event time from the start, with first-class watermarks, event-time timers, and rich keyed-state primitives like value, list, and map state through process functions, so sophisticated stateful logic and fine-grained temporal rules are natural, and its checkpointing and savepoints give strong exactly-once with low overhead. Spark supports event time, watermarks, and stateful operations too, and they are good, but the state model and timer control are less granular than Flink's.

The counterweight is Spark's ecosystem and unification. Because Spark is batch-first and its streaming uses the same DataFrame and SQL API as batch, a team already running heavy batch ETL, Spark SQL, and Spark ML gets streaming as an extension of the same engine, the same code, and the same skills, and it has a larger community, more connectors, and deep integration with Delta Lake and Databricks. So the choice is rarely about raw capability, since both handle most streaming tasks, but about fit. I pick Flink when I need the lowest latency, the richest state and event-time semantics, or complex event processing, and I pick Spark Structured Streaming when I want one engine and one skill set across batch, analytics, machine learning, and streaming, or the organization is already invested in Spark and Databricks. I also weigh operational maturity, because running Flink well is its own discipline while a Spark shop can extend into streaming with less new burden.

At the National Bank of India we actually used both, deliberately. For sub-second fraud reaction on the live transaction stream, where every millisecond counts and the rule needs detailed per-account state and timers, we used Flink because its true record-at-a-time model and rich keyed state fit exactly. For a near-real-time transaction-volume dashboard that lived alongside our large Spark batch and analytics stack, we used Spark Structured Streaming because its micro-batch latency was perfectly acceptable there and it ran on the same engine, the same DataFrame code, and the same Delta and Databricks ecosystem as the rest of our analytics, so there was no new engine to operate. That is my summary: Flink for the hard, low-latency, heavily stateful streaming, and Spark Structured Streaming for streaming that benefits from unification with batch and analytics in an existing ecosystem.
